source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: GPT-4 agent in Minecraft stores working code as skills in a library, retrieved by description. It beat ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGPT on exploration and tech-tree speed.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations (3.3x more than baselines); 2.3x longer distances. Tech tree, iterations to unlock (3 runs each): wooden 6+-2 vs AutoGPT 92+-72; stone 11+-2 vs 94+-72; iron 21+-7 vs 135+-103; diamond only Voyager (1/3 runs, 102 iterations). ReAct and Reflexion 0/3 on all levels.
limits: Only 3 runs per method. Skills are verified by execution plus a GPT-4 self-check. Read through the arXiv HTML page via a summarizer, first 100k of 150k characters.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of a Soar chunk: a verified result from a hard sub-problem is stored and called later. Supports schema S9 memory, but only when each skill passed an execution check first.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager, zero-shot generalization table
finding: In a fresh Minecraft world, the skill library is what carries over. Even AutoGPT improves when handed Voyager's library.
numbers: Iterations to finish (successes of 3): Voyager diamond pickaxe 19+-3 (3/3), golden sword 18+-7 (3/3), lava bucket 21+-5 (3/3), compass 18+-2 (3/3). Voyager without skill library: 36 (2/3), 30+-9, 27+-9, 26+-3. AutoGPT 0/3 on all four. AutoGPT with Voyager library: 39 (1/3), 30 (1/3), 0/3, 30 (2/3).
limits: Four tasks, three runs each. Library came from the same game, so this is transfer inside one domain.
agent_relevance: Measured transfer: a stored library cuts time to solution by roughly 30-45% on new tasks and makes some unsolvable tasks solvable. Chunks move between agents when they are plain, runnable code.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager, ablations
finding: The verification step and the curriculum mattered more than the library alone. Without the skill library, progress plateaus late.
numbers: Random curriculum: discovered items down 93%. No self-verification: down 73%. GPT-3.5 instead of GPT-4 for code: GPT-4 gives 5.7x more unique items. No-library variant reached early tech levels at similar speed (wooden 7+-2, stone 9+-4, iron 29+-11) but never the diamond tool.
limits: Ablation curves are in a figure; the library effect has no single number. Single environment.
agent_relevance: Learning from an impasse only pays if the stored result is checked (G3). A library without verification is a risk, not a gain. The library's value shows late and on hard goals, not early.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024; ICML 2025) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: An LM induces reusable sub-routines (workflows) from past trajectories and adds them to memory. Works offline from training data and online from the agent's own test runs.
numbers: WebArena (812 tasks, gpt-4-0613, temp 0): success 35.5% vs BrowserGym baseline 23.5% (+12.0 points, +51.1% relative); about 2.0 fewer steps per task (5.9 steps). Beat SteP with 14 human-written workflows (32.0) by 7.6% relative. Mind2Web cross-task step success 45.1 vs 36.2, task success 4.8 vs 2.0.
limits: Table text extraction was garbled; baseline numbers taken from the paper's prose. Online mode learns from model-predicted success, which can be wrong.
agent_relevance: Direct measure that induced procedure memory raises success and cuts steps without training. A 12-point gain at equal model is the size of effect a scaffold memory can hope for.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, generalization tests
finding: Transfer gets weaker as the gap between where workflows came from and where they are used grows, yet online induction still helps.
numbers: Mind2Web step success, MindAct vs AWM-offline vs AWM-online (GPT-4): cross-task 36.2 / 45.1 / 43.6; cross-website 30.1 / 33.7 / 33.9; cross-domain 18.6 / 32.6 / 35.5. Whole-task success stays at 0.7 to 4.8%. WebArena cross-template subset: AWM 33.2 vs BrowserGym 20.5.
limits: Mind2Web whole-task success is tiny, so step gains do not mean the task gets done. Offline cross-domain action F1 fell (52.8 to 41.6).
agent_relevance: A stored routine helps even in a new domain, but mostly at step level. Our agent should measure whole-task success on a held-out set, not step scores (G3, G7).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, induction variants
finding: Abstract sub-routine workflows from an LM beat raw copied action sequences on Mind2Web and tie on WebArena. This is the generality question of chunking in LLM form.
numbers: WebArena: rule-based induction 35.6% success, 6.3 steps; LM-based 35.5%, 5.9 steps. Mind2Web cross-task: rule-based element accuracy 49.5, step success 43.4; LM-based 50.6 and 45.1; task success 2.0 vs 4.8.
limits: WebArena difference is 0.1 point, within noise. Offline workflows from mismatched training examples can degrade online use (authors' text).
agent_relevance: Generalize the stored procedure (drop example-specific values) but keep it concrete enough to run. Same trade-off as over-specific versus over-general chunks. Evidence is thin: one tie, one small gain.

source: Wang, Gandhi, Neubig, Fried (2025) Inducing Programmatic Skills for Agentic Tasks (ASI)
finding: Agent induces program skills, runs them as a check, and keeps only the ones that pass. Compared with vanilla and with text workflows (AWM).
numbers: WebArena (812 tasks, Claude-3.5-Sonnet): vanilla 32.7%, AWM 36.3%, ASI 40.4% (+23.5% relative over vanilla, +11.3% over AWM). Steps 5.6 / 5.9 / 5.0. GPT-4o vanilla 12.3%, GPT-4o AWM 35.5%.
limits: Text states some numbers that disagree with tables (step-reduction ratios reversed; 4.2 vs 3.8 points). Only 15.6% of turns produced a program that passed verification.
agent_relevance: Adding execution verification before storing beats storing unchecked text. Same lesson as G3: a stored result needs a pass on something real.

source: Wang et al. (2025) ASI, verification ablation (Shopping split)
finding: Verification helps; program form helps a bit; putting skills in the action space beats leaving them in memory text.
numbers: Shopping success: unverified text memory 32.6; verified program in memory 36.4; verified text memory 39.0; verified program as action 40.1 (main table gives 40.4). Verification gain stated as 4.2 points; table difference is 3.8.
limits: One site split; no variance reported. Agents sometimes tried to call a program that was only in memory.
agent_relevance: Storing a skill is not enough; it must be callable. Verified plus executable beats unverified text by about 7.5 points here.

source: Wang et al. (2025) ASI, cross-website transfer and failures
finding: Skills induced on a sandbox site carry to the real site, and an update step repairs ones that break. Some skills break on layout change.
numbers: 10 queries per site pair. Success, vanilla / AWM / ASI: Shopping 80.0 / 80.0 / 90.0; Reddit 40.0 / 56.7 / 76.7; Map 63.3 / 100.0 / 93.3. ASI vs AWM success not significant (t=-1.398, p=0.167); step reduction significant (p=0.038).
limits: Tiny sample (10 per cell). A sort_by_listings() skill broke on a different layout. Agents under-used new skills because the search space was large.
agent_relevance: Transfer is real but untested at power. Skills need a precondition and a repair path, like Soar chunks that carry conditions.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) SkillWeaver: Web Agents can Self-Improve by Discovering and Honing Skills
finding: Agent explores a site, practices skills, and writes them as APIs. APIs written by a strong agent help a weaker one.
numbers: WebArena average success: GPT-4o 22.6 to 29.8 (+32% relative); GPT-4o-mini 9.2 to 14.1 with transferred skills (+45%). Online-Mind2Web, 57 tasks over 4 sites: 40.2 to 56.2 (+40% relative; Flights 11.7 to 29.4, Cars 11.1 to 11.1). Abstract says up to 54.3% for weaker agents, a figure not in Table 1.
limits: Abstract and tables disagree (31.8 vs 32; 39.8 vs 40; 54.3 vs 45). Real-site samples are 8 to 23 tasks. Weaker model misused APIs (wrong parameters, wrong pick). Read first 100k of 138k characters.
agent_relevance: A procedure compiled by a stronger run can be reused by a weaker run. Useful if our scaffold ever splits roles, but the weaker model still fails at calling the skill correctly.

source: SkillsBench (2026) Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks
finding: Human-curated skills help a lot. Skills written by the model itself give no gain. This is the cleanest test of self-compiled procedures.
numbers: 84 tasks, 11 domains, 7 agent-model setups over 3 harnesses, 7,308 valid trajectories. Pass rate 24.3% no skills, 40.6% curated (+16.2 points), self-generated about -1.3 points (range -5.6 for GPT-5.2 to +1.4 for Opus 4.6). Haiku 4.5 with skills 27.7% beats Opus 4.5 without (22.0%).
quote: Self-generated Skills provide negligible or negative benefit.
limits: Abstract says 86 tasks, body says 84. Skills add context, and there is no length-matched control. Terminal tasks only. Curated skills scored 10.1/12 on quality vs 6.2/12 for the wider ecosystem.
agent_relevance: Strongest warning for us: a model cannot reliably write its own procedure memory before use. A chunk must come from a checked trace, not from the model's summary. Supports G2 and G3.

source: SkillsBench (2026), breakdowns
finding: Gains depend on domain, count and length of skills. More or longer is not better.
numbers: Domain gain: Healthcare +51.9, Manufacturing +41.9, Math +6.0, Software Engineering +4.5. 16 of 84 tasks got worse with skills. Skills per task: 1 skill +17.8, 2-3 skills +18.6, 4+ skills +5.9. Length: detailed +18.8 (N=1,165), compact +17.1 (N=845), standard +10.1 (N=773), comprehensive -2.9 (N=140).
limits: Observational cuts of the same data, not randomized. Domains with weak pre-training coverage gain most.
agent_relevance: Keep stored procedures short and few (1-3 per problem). Matches the Soar lesson that many or large chunks cost more than they give (utility problem).

source: Skills in the wild (2026) How Well Do Agentic Skills Work in the Wild: Benchmarking LLM Skill Usage in Realistic Settings
finding: With a pool of 34,198 real skills and retrieval, the benefit shrinks toward the no-skill level. The agent loads fewer skills and gets noisy ones.
numbers: SkillsBench (84 tasks) pass rate, Claude Opus 4.6 / Kimi K2.5 / Qwen3.5: no skills 35.4 / 21.8 / 20.5; curated 51.2 / 38.9 / 31.6; curated plus distractors (Opus) 43.5; retrieved with curated 40.1 / 33.5 / 26.7; retrieved without curated 38.4 / 19.8 / 19.7. Opus skill-loading rate 62.2% curated vs 44.4% retrieved.
limits: Each condition run 3 times. Qwen numbers are inconsistent between text and table. Three models only. Author names not recorded.
agent_relevance: The retrieval step is the weak point of a large library: Soar had this as match cost and wrong firing. Keep the library small and selected by code (G5).

source: Skills in the wild (2026), refinement results
finding: Rewriting retrieved skills for the specific task recovers part of the loss when the skills are already roughly relevant. It does not help when they are not.
numbers: Terminal-Bench 2.0 (89 tasks), Opus / Kimi / Qwen: no skills 57.7 / 46.6 / 44.7; retrieved 61.4 / 50.6 / 44.2; query-specific refinement 65.5 / 56.2 / 49.1. SkillsBench retrieved with curated, Opus: 40.1 to 48.2 with query-specific refinement; without curated: 38.4 to 37.9. Kimi dropped 33.5 to 26.7 in one refined setting.
limits: Refinement results mixed across models. Query-agnostic needs sub-agents, absent for Kimi.
agent_relevance: Specializing a stored routine to the present problem (like Soar re-instantiating a chunk with current values) works only when the routine already fits.

source: Feng, Bijoy, Balasubramanian, Zhou (2026) Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents
finding: Skills induced from whole tasks often hurt the agent that retrieves them. Skills induced per sub-task help on average. This is chunk grain size, tested.
numbers: 11 models, 3 benchmarks (AppWorld, OfficeBench, KramaBench). One Average row over 11 models: task-level none 22.1, +text 20.9, +code 18.0; subtask-level none 24.8, +text 26.7, +code 25.3. Text beat code by 2.9 points (task-level) and 1.4 (subtask-level). GPT-OSS-120B on AppWorld fell from 27.3% to 1.0% with task-level code skills; in 69% of those runs it called the stored whole-task function and stopped within 2 steps.
limits: The Average row shown may be for one benchmark block; could not tell which from the extracted text. Tool-use and data tasks, not reasoning puzzles.
agent_relevance: Store sub-goal results (a chunk of a substate), not whole-task answers. Whole-task memory is an over-specific chunk and lowers success below no-memory. Strong support for S9 holding sub-procedures only.

source: Feng et al. (2026) Break It Down, Pass It On, skill utility score
finding: A skill's usefulness depends on both closeness to real tasks (specificity) and spread over tasks (abstractness). The product of the two predicts success.
numbers: Success rises across 10 retrieved-utility bins from 14.0% to 24.5% (task-level agent) and from 22.8% to 31.0% (subtask-level). Median split of the library: high-utility half beats low half, e.g. AppWorld task-level 15.4 vs 10.2, KramaBench task-level 30.3 vs 26.0, subtask-level 34.0 vs 31.5; another pair 38.3 vs 36.9 with overlapping intervals.
limits: Score uses embeddings of skill and task text; some high-versus-low gaps sit inside the 95% intervals.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap code-side filter for admitting a chunk: neither too narrow nor too broad. Could replace a model judge of chunk quality (G5).

source: Xiong et al. (2025; ACL 2026) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Agents copy the outputs of similar stored experiences, so wrong stored items spread. Adding everything lowers accuracy; adding only checked items raises it.
numbers: Four agents (RegAgent 4,000 runs; EHRAgent 2,392; AgentDriver 2,000; CIC-IoT 1,000), GPT-4o-mini. Score, fixed memory / add-all / strict-add: 67.53 / 55.48 / 70.95; 16.75 / 13.05 / 38.50; 40.11 / 32.32 / 51.00; 71.50 / 59.90 / 85.40. RegAgent input-output similarity correlation near 1.
limits: Strict add uses a correctness evaluator. Coarse evaluators gave mixed results; only one fine-tuned on 300 trajectories beat fixed memory consistently. Author names not recorded.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for the wrong-chunk problem: once a bad item is stored it gets reused. Admission by a real check beats storing every episode (G2, G3).

source: Xiong et al. (2025) Experience-Following, deletion and misaligned replay
finding: Pruning old records by later usefulness gives small gains, and a noisy judge can delete good records.
numbers: Deleted records had lower correctness than retained ones: EHRAgent (4o-mini judge) retained 44.1 vs deleted 36.3; CIC-IoT 78.9 vs 56.7. Strict evaluator: history deletion about +1.8 points average over no deletion (range -1.15 to +4.20); combined deletion about -0.4 while cutting memory 70-79% (these averages are the fetch summary's own calculation). With a noisy judge, AgentDriver dropped from 36.92 to 34.00.
limits: Averages are a derived calculation. On AgentDriver the retained records were not better than deleted ones.
agent_relevance: Forgetting is cheap and keeps accuracy about level, which helps the budget. But deletion needs a reliable signal or it removes useful chunks.

source: Zhao et al. (2024, AAAI) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: Agent writes cross-task insights from success and failure pairs and also recalls successful trajectories; no weight updates.
numbers: ALFWorld success: ReAct 40.0, ExpeL 59.0, insights-only 50, retrieval-only 55; random retrieval 42.5. HotpotQA: ReAct 28.0, ExpeL 39.0, insights-only 36, retrieval-only 31, hand-written insights 32.0, insights beside reflections 29.0. WebShop mean reward 0.666 (ReAct) vs 0.701 (ExpeL). Insights from gpt-3.5 gave 32.0 on HotpotQA vs 39.0 from gpt-4.
limits: Closed API models only, text only. Insight quality depends on the extraction model (7-point gap).
agent_relevance: Two kinds of stored experience (rule-like insights and raw cases) each add; combined is best. Insight quality tracks model strength, so a weak model should not write its own rules unchecked.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL, transfer test
finding: Insights from HotpotQA carried to FEVER with only a small adaptation.
numbers: FEVER success: Act 58, ReAct 63, ExpeL transfer without task demos 65 (+-1.7), ExpeL transfer 70 (+-0.7). On ALFWorld at Reflexion round 3: ReAct+Reflexion 54.4% vs ExpeL+Reflexion 64.2%.
limits: Two related QA-style tasks; effect 2 to 7 points. The effect of number of training tasks was not on the page read.
agent_relevance: Small but positive cross-task transfer of general insights. Test our own store the same way: learn on set A, score on unrelated set B.

source: Fan, Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: A Mechanism-Level Review
finding: Maps Soar chunking to Reflexion and AgentHER at evidence level E3 (functional match), depth D4, and says the key piece is missing: compilation from the dependency structure of a scoped impasse resolution. Voyager, AWM and SGDR are coded E3/D4 for workflow induction.
numbers: Reviews 10 historical architectures, 8 runtime families, 42 modern systems. One of five residual gaps is typed impasse with isolated substates and resolution compilation. GraSP is said to already cover calibrated skill selection, compilation, verification and repair.
limits: A review coded by its authors, not a test. Read by targeted search of the extracted text, not cover to cover.
agent_relevance: Confirms no known LLM agent does chunking proper (condition-aware compilation after an impasse). Open design slot for us, and a risk of building something unvalidated.

source: CogRec (2025) A Cognitive Recommender Agent Fusing Large Language Models and Soar for Explainable Recommendation
finding: Soar runs the loop. On a tie impasse it asks an LLM, then Soar chunking turns the answer into a rule. Tested on three public recommendation datasets (ML-1M, Movies, Yelp).
numbers: Ablations are in a figure: without chunking, performance degrades 'approaching' LLM-Direct; without LLM bootstrap, a 'drastic' drop; LLM call frequency falls to a low stable plateau with chunking and stays high without it. About 500 bootstrap rules. Table 2 headline gains of 4.1% to 9.1% over the best baseline, but the extracted table was garbled.
quote: enabling it to transform transient solutions into permanent, reusable skills
limits: No call counts as numbers. Table columns and baseline names misaligned, so exact comparisons are uncertain. Authors built the setup; no independent replication.
agent_relevance: Only end-to-end use found of impasse-triggered LLM call plus chunking. The measured benefit (fewer LLM calls over time) is the cost argument for compiling; the accuracy numbers are weak evidence.

source: NL2GenSym (2025) Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR via Large Language Models
finding: Generator-critic loop turns natural-language descriptions into Soar rules, executed in Soar for feedback. It beats one-shot prompting and, on success rate, manual rules.
numbers: Water-jug dataset. Success rate: manual 84%; Gemini-2.5-pro zero-shot 0%, one-shot 55%, framework 86%; Qwen-max zero-shot 0%, one-shot 66%, framework 91%. Hard cases: manual 46.67%, one-shot Gemini 20%, framework Gemini 76.67%. Decision cycles near 1.5x optimum on hard cases, versus thousands for manual and one-shot rules.
limits: One puzzle family; authors' own dataset; no independent test.
agent_relevance: Zero-shot LLM rule writing got 0%; execution feedback was needed. Same as G2: models fix well once shown a failing real output.

source: NL2GenSym (2025) ablation
finding: The execution-grounded Critic is the most important part. A small model plus the framework beat a larger model with one-shot prompting.
numbers: Removing the Critic: overall success down 23%, hard and variant cases down 37%, decision cycles above 1,000x optimum. Removing the Basic Knowledge Base: down 17%. Removing the Case Knowledge Base: down 14%. Gemini-Flash with framework 86% vs Gemini-Pro one-shot 55%.
limits: Percentages are success-rate points on a small test set; the Case KB ablation kept the first case.
agent_relevance: Feedback from real execution outweighs a bigger model for writing rules. A store of past cases adds about 14 points.

source: Kirk, Wray, Laird (2023; AAAI-SS 2024) Exploiting Language Models as a Source of Knowledge for Cognitive Agents
finding: Position paper from the Soar group: use an LLM as a knowledge source for a cognitive-architecture agent and combine extraction with architecture capabilities. Only the abstract page was read.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Abstract only. A 2025 survey (as quoted by search) says LLM-Soar integration work is mostly conceptual and lacks robust validation.
agent_relevance: The Soar group's own framing: LLM as a source of knowledge at the impasse, architecture decides what to keep.

source: Taatgen, Lee (2003) Production Compilation: A Simple Mechanism to Model Complex Skill Acquisition
finding: ACT-R model learns by combining two rules that fire in sequence into one specialized rule. Applied to the Kanfer-Ackerman air traffic control task, it matches human practice curves at three levels.
numbers: Human data: 65 undergraduates, 18 trials of 10 min, trials 1-10 compared. Planes landed per trial r2=.97; land-unit task r2=.98; other levels r2=.91 and .87. Model was faster than people at the start.
limits: Model starts with all declarative knowledge, so it beats people early. Fitted to one task. Not an LLM.
agent_relevance: Machine proof that compile-by-merging two steps gives a human-like speed-up. The LLM analogue is merging a retrieval step into the rule that uses it.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere, Anderson (ACT-R modeling paradigms chapter) and Taatgen & Lee (2003), on chunking problems
finding: States two known flaws of earlier compilers: chunking sometimes made rules that were too general, and both Soar and ACT* made growing macro-procedures that are costly to match. Production compilation avoids this by merging only two rules at a time.
numbers: Cites Tambe, Newell, Rosenbloom (1990) for match cost. No new numbers. ACT-R still over-generalizes through old-experience strategies (a DC-10 landing example).
quote: it sometimes produced procedures that were too general
limits: Claim comes from a competing-theory paper; ACT-R authors argue for their own mechanism.
agent_relevance: Two failure modes to guard: over-general and over-large. Small steps (two-step merges) and short stored procedures are the safer design.

source: Soar Manual, chapter 4: Procedural Knowledge Learning (explanatory chunking)
finding: Current Soar chunking builds rules from a behavior trace with identity analysis. A rule is over-general if it applies where the original reasoning would not. Known sources of wrong chunks are listed.
numbers: Learning is off by default. Named risks: operator-selection knowledge (add-osk off by default), random or numerically chosen operators, local negations, no-change impasse results, knowledge recalled from semantic or episodic memory. Hundreds of firings can compress into one.
quote: the learned rule produces the exact same results that the original problem-solving would have produced
limits: First 100,000 of 140,700 characters read through a summarizer, so the quote may be paraphrased. No empirical benchmark numbers.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready correctness test for any compiled rule: replay and compare with the original result. Also lists when NOT to compile: stochastic choices, memory recalled into the substate.

source: More Skills, Worse Agents? (2026 workshop paper, as described in a search result)
finding: Reported by a search summary only: growing the skill library degrades performance, with skill shadowing (wrong skill chosen) as the main cause rather than context length.
numbers: Up to 21% drop from a small helpful set to a 202-skill library (search summary; not verified).
limits: Not opened and not verified. URL points to a related paper, not this one. Listed because it matches the utility problem in Soar.
agent_relevance: If verified, supports capping library size and using code-side selection.

source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1986) Chunking in Soar: The Anatomy of a General Learning Mechanism
finding: Original description: chunking turns goal-based problem-solving experience into new rules, shown on macro-operators and search control. Only the abstract record was seen.
numbers: None read.
limits: Full PDF download failed (disk full). Over-general and expensive-chunk claims were not in what I read. Newell and Rosenbloom (1981) power law was not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Foundation for the schema idea that a substate result becomes a stored rule.
